https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c74g.text: Image source, Basarnas Image caption, KMP Mutiara Sentosa 2 ferry with thick plumes of smoke billowing from behind By Olivia Ireland Published 2 August 2026, 11:02 BST Updated 1 hour ago Five people have been found dead and 41 are missing after an Indonesian ferry carrying at least 250 people caught fire while at sea, officials say. The captain of the ship reported the fire - off Madura island - as the vessel sailed from the country's second-largest city, Surabaya in East Java, to Makassar in South Sulawesi, according to Basarnas, the National Search and Rescue Agency. Footage played by local Indonesian news outlet iNews shows large numbers of people in life jackets on what appears to be a lifeboat. Other clips show people climbing down from the ferry that has flames and plumes of smoke coming from the top of the vessel. Basarnas posted a video to its TikTok, with a statement saying at 08:24 (02:24 GMT) the Surabaya Search and Rescue office received information that passenger ship KMP Mutiara Sentosa 2 was on fire. "Based on information from the shipping company, the fire occurred at around 06:00-07:00 (00:00-01:00 GMT)." Later, Basarnas said it got confirmation the ferry "was almost entirely engulfed in flames" as "passengers held on in the ship's bridge and bow while awaiting rescue". It was unclear how the ferry caught fire, the statement said. In some of the footage, can be seen jumping into the sea, with crowds of people in life jackets gathering and lifebuoys being thrown to some before they are carried into a rescue ship. https://www.politico.eu/article/finance-.text: LUXEMBOURG — EU finance ministers struck a compromise to beef up the bloc’s markets watchdog Friday, but the deal exposed divisions over national control and exemptions that critics say favor the biggest member countries. Most finance ministers backed the Council’s position on MISP, a package of bills to integrate and police financial markets. At its heart is a plan to give the EU’s securities regulator powers to oversee major financial players — a flagship bid to make Europe a stronger investment hub, where European companies can seek investors without traveling to Wall Street. But capitals stopped short of handing the future watchdog too much autonomy, triggering a hard rebuke from the European Commission. Advertisement Advertisement “We deeply regret that the compromise now on the table falls significantly short of the level of ambition needed,” Finance Commissioner Maria Luís Albuquerque told ministers during Friday’s public Ecofin debate in Luxembourg. “We need [the European Securities and Markets Authority] to become an effective supervisor. The current compromise text would not allow for that.” France spearheaded a last-minute push over dinner Thursday to strengthen the watchdog’s executive powers. Paris took issue with a rule that would allow nine national supervisors to force the watchdog’s executive board to submit draft decisions for further scrutiny before they’re adopted. The Irish EU presidency tweaked the rule overnight to limit national supervisors’ ability to delay decisions and preserve the watchdog’s power to act in emergencies, according to a compromise document obtained by POLITICO. That was enough for France and most other countries. But not for the Commission, nor European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde, who was equally critical of the Council compromise. Beyond the governance concerns, Albuquerque took aim at supervisory carve-outs that the Irish introduced to accommodate Germany’s push to exclude its stock exchange, Deutsche Börse, from EU oversight. The carve-out club The carve-out shields stock exchanges from direct EU supervision unless they meet certain thresholds for trading activity and cross-border reach. Spain’s stock exchange, Bolsas y Mercados Españoles, would also benefit from the carve-outs, triggering criticism from smaller EU countries that accused the waiver of granting the bloc’s largest nations preferential treatment. Belgium was particularly critical because its Brussels-based securities depository Euroclear is expected to come under direct EU oversight and face supervisory fees, while some major stock exchanges could remain under national oversight. Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever will take the issue to EU leaders at the end of next week. “We cannot support the carve-outs. The package includes as many ins as there are outs,” Belgian Finance Minister Jan Jambon said during Friday’s public debate. “I think Germany has won in certain cases.” Advertisement Advertisement As a peace offering, Berlin backed a review clause that would allow the Commission to revisit the carve-outs two years after the supervisory rules start applying. Any changes would require new legislation, however. “The carve-out is temporary,” Dutch Finance Minister Eelco Heinen, who backed the deal, told journalists Thursday. “If that exchange were to grow, it would also fall under [EU supervision]. This is also intended to ensure that Dutch companies or pan-European companies such as Euronext are not put at a disadvantage.” Friday’s deal puts pressure on MEPs to agree Parliament’s position so negotiations on a final text can begin. The Commission hopes future legislative negotiations will provide a second chance to improve the text, which also threatens to increase pressure on the EU budget. Under the compromise, the EU budget would shoulder 60% of the cost of ESMA’s activities not covered by industry fees, with national supervisors paying the remaining 40%. “The Commission cannot accept a significant increase in the EU budget contribution in light of the difficult discussion at [the Multiannual Financial Framework ],” Albuquerque said amid a bitter budget battle that threatens to shave hundreds of billions of euros off the proposed €2 trillion cash pot. “I sincerely hope that the European Parliament will be more ambitious.”

https://www.readingeagle.com/2026/11/10/.text: Family members of Holocaust survivors light memorial candles during a Prayers of Remembrance Service, an interfaith liturgy to commemorate Kristallnacht and Yom Hashoah at Christ Episcopal Church, Fifth and Court streets, on Monday, Nov. 9, 2026. (BILL UHRICH/READING EAGLE) By Bill Uhrich | buhrich@readingeagle.com | Reading Eagle PUBLISHED: November 10, 2026 at 11:45 AM EST | UPDATED: November 10, 2026 at 12:45 PM EST Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... On the minds of many of the more than 150 worshippers who gathered Monday night at Christ Episcopal Church in Reading were the events leading up to Sunday’s protests in Philadelphia surrounding six Jewish-owned restaurants. According to the The Philadelphia Inquirer , police estimated 300 pro-Palestinian protesters and 200 counterprotesters confronted one another on the eve of the anniversary of Kristallnacht — the Night of Broken Glass, when Nazi Germany launched pogroms against Jews on the night of Nov. 9-10, 1938, a precursor to the Holocaust. The Inquirer noted that hundreds of others patronized the businesses in solidarity. Sunday’s protests were an unsettling background to the annual interfaith commemoration on the anniversary of Kristallnacht held at Christ Episcopal as a remembrance of the victims of the Holocaust. Cantor and Rabbi Ted Prosnitz of Kesher Zion Synagogue, Wyomissing, acknowledged that tension before singing “Es Brint — Our Town Burns,” a song composed following a pogrom in the Polish town of Pizytik in 1938. Rabbi Brian I. Michelson of Reform Congregation Oheb Sholom, left, and Kesher Zion Synagogue Cantor/Rabbi Ted Prosnitz recite the traditional Jewish prayer for the dead, during a Reading interfaith service Monday to commemorate Kristallnacht and Yom Hashoah at Christ Episcopal Church. (BILL UHRICH/READING EAGLE) “Our gathering here tonight, and this song in particular, are especially poignant,” he said. “When the fire of hatred is allowed to spread unchecked, the fire of hatred promoted just yesterday in Philadelphia, that fire can burn down an entire society, but people here tonight and people in Philadelphia on Sunday stood up. “They heeded the warning.” Begun at Christ Episcopal in 1995, the annual service of remembrance had included members of Trinity Lutheran Church in Reading and the Reading Jewish community. Today it brings together the Jewish Federation of Reading/Berks, Reform Congregation Oheb Sholom and Kesher Zion along with Christ Episcopal and the Greater Reading Unity Coalition, consisting of the federation, Reading Branch NAACP, the Daniel Torres Hispanic Center, Islamic Center of Reading and the LGBT Center of Greater Reading. The Rev. Bryce Wandrey, rector at Christ Episcopal, opened the service with a prayer. “We gather this evening, as we have done for many years, to lament the tragedy of Kristallnacht and to mark Yom Hashoah, the act of remembering all Jewish people who died in the Holocaust,” he said. “But we also gather, as we always do, in order to strengthen our bonds of unity,” he said. Family members of Holocaust survivor Esther Bratt, center, gather with her following a Prayers of Remembrance Service, an interfaith liturgy to commemorate Kristallnacht and Yom Hashoah at Christ Episcopal Church, Fifth and Court streets, on Monday, Nov. 9, 2026. From left are Andy and Corinne Wernick, daughter and son-in-law of Bratt; Esther Bratt; Leah Leisawitz, 14, great-granddaughter of Bratt; and Michele Leisawitz, granddaughter of Bratt. (BILL UHRICH/READING EAGLE) Michele Leisawitz, granddaughter of Holocaust survivors Esther Bratt and the late Sidney Bratt, who died in 2024 at age 96, was in attendance with her family. “It’s really a scary time,” she said following the service. “I think people really need to remember and never forget, and that’s more important today than ever.” She was proud to see so many people coming out in support during the protests in Philadelphia against hate and antisemitism. “They showed our community the support that we really appreciated,” she said. “And I think that’s a major difference between now and when Kristallnacht happened. We didn’t have that support.” Leisawitz explained that her grandmother didn’t experience Kristallnacht, but she was in the Jewish ghetto of Vilna, now in Lithuania. She and Sidney, also a Holocaust survivor, attended the remembrance service from its start. Now, Esther, 97, takes part in the service with her extended family. “Sid actually witnessed the burning of the synagogues,” she said. Worshippers hold candles during a Prayers of Remembrance Service, an interfaith liturgy to commemorate Kristallnacht and Yom Hashoah at Christ Episcopal Church, Fifth and Court streets, on Monday, Nov. 9, 2026. (BILL UHRICH/READING EAGLE) Her great-granddaughter Leah Leisawitz, 14, represents a new generation learning about her family’s history and the necessity of belonging to a community like that which participated in the remembrance service. “With everything going on, I am scared, and it is a scary time,” she said while sitting next to her great-grandmother. “And these events with everybody coming out, it’s a reminder how all these people are here for you, and that you do have a community, an amazing community, that is here to support you through this hard time.” Prior to the service, a Circle of Light candlelight vigil was held outside the church in the first block of North Fifth Street. John Morgan, a member of the Greater Reading Unity Coalition, welcomed the participants. “We are gathered here together,” he said, “as a visible sign that light is more powerful than darkness, love more powerful than hate, peace more powerful than violence.” Worshippers gather in a Circle of Light and pray led by John Morgan of the Greater Reading Unity Coalition, prior to a Prayers of Remembrance Service, an interfaith liturgy to commemorate Kristallnacht and Yom Hashoah at Christ Episcopal Church, Fifth and Court streets, on Monday, Nov. 9, 2026.
